text.em-dash-density	markdown	The hook runs first — before the guard — and then the mod reads the result — once. The guard reads each command before the shell sees it. The shell then runs only what the guard allowed. When the guard blocks a command, the agent gets a short message that names the reason. The agent can change the command and try again. Nothing runs in the meantime. The mod listens for the same event and writes a line to the status pane. The pane shows the last few commands and how each one ended. A person can open the pane at any time to see what the agents are doing. Each entry carries the agent name, the folder it works in and the time it started. Old entries drop off the list after a day. The settings file holds the switch for the pane, and the default is on. Setup asks about it once and records the answer. Removing the plugin removes the pane as well. The pane never stores the text of a command. It keeps only the first word and the exit code. That keeps secrets out of the list. The list lives in memory and is gone when the session ends.
text.triad-density	markdown	Plans, specs and roadmaps go to the planner. Pages, themes and widgets go to the designer. Tests, builds and releases go to the runner. The lead reads each report before it assigns the next step. A report names the files that changed and the checks that ran. When a check fails, the report says which one and shows the shortest line that explains it. The lead then decides whether to resume the same agent or to start a fresh one. A fresh agent starts with only the brief it is given. A resumed agent keeps what it already learned. Each choice has a cost, and the lead picks the cheaper one for the job at hand. Small fixes go to the agent that wrote the code. A change that touches a new area goes to a new agent with a clear brief. The brief names the goal and the files in scope. It says what done looks like. It says which tests prove it. Agents work in separate folders so that two of them never edit the same file. When both finish, the lead merges the branches one at a time. After each merge the lead reruns the checks that cover the merged files. If a check fails, the lead sends the failure back to the agent that owns the change. The agent fixes it and reports again. This loop repeats until every check is green. Only then does the lead open the pull request. The pull request body lists what changed and why. It also lists anything left undone. Reviewers read the body first and the diff second. They leave comments on the lines they question. The author answers each comment with a change or a reason. When every comment is settled, the branch is merged into the main line. The team then deletes the branch and the folder that held it. Nothing from the old folder is kept. The notes that matter live in the project memory instead. Each note is short and has a single topic. A note says why the fact matters, so a later reader can judge whether it still holds. Anyone who joins later can read those notes and catch up in an afternoon.
